title: Put a returned box back into its place in a size run
instruction: Put the blue box back into the shelf channel in front of the right arm, between the red and green boxes, so the row reads red, blue, green from its left end, closed up with every box standing against the back.
context: Shoe and apparel stockrooms keep each style in a size run so a picker grabs the right size without reading labels; a returned box must go back into its place in the run, shifting the larger sizes along, not be parked at the end of the row. Done by: retail stock associates, stockroom and warehouse order pickers.
setup: A grey painted steel shelf channel is fixed to the table in front of the right arm, running left to right: a floor strip 22 cm long, 5 cm deep and 5 mm thick, a back stop 1 cm thick along its far edge and an end stop 1 cm thick at each end, all three rising 3 cm above the strip; the back stop is 24 cm long, spanning the strip and both end stops, and each end stop is 5 cm long, the strip's depth. The channel's inside runs from 6 cm to 28 cm right of the midline between the arm bases; the strip's front edge is 23.1 cm and the back stop's face 28.1 cm in front of the arm bases. Three identical cardboard boxes, 4 cm front to back, 6 cm left to right and 9 cm tall, 150 g each, stand upright with their 6 cm side along the row; their colour marks the size: red small, blue medium, green large. The red box stands in the channel 1 mm from the left end stop and 1 mm from the back stop, its centre 9.1 cm right of the midline and 26 cm in front of the arm bases. The green box stands 1 mm to the right of the red box, the same distance from the back stop, its centre 15.2 cm right of the midline. An orange rubber return mat (10 x 10 cm, 3 mm thick) is fixed to the table in front of the left arm, its centre 25 cm left of the midline and 26 cm in front of the arm bases; the blue box stands on its centre. The left arm cannot reach the channel and the right arm cannot reach the mat. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: A box stands in the channel when its centre is over the floor strip (or within 5 mm past its outline), its bottom is within 5 mm of the strip's top, and it is tilted at most 10 degrees. 0.1 when the gap between the red and green boxes is at least 6 cm (the blue box's width), or the blue box stands between them. 0.5 when the blue box stands in the channel between the red and green boxes, so the row reads red, blue, green from the left. With that, 0.2 when the red box is within 5 mm of the left end stop and both gaps between neighbouring boxes are 5 mm or less; and 0.2 when, for every box, both bottom corners of its back face are within 5 mm of the back stop's face, measured at the bottom of the box. The back face is the box's 6 cm x 9 cm face towards the stop, so each box must stand with its 6 cm side along the row: a box turned a quarter turn, with a 4 cm end towards the stop, gets no back credit, and since the two corners are 6 cm apart, a box turned more than 4.8 degrees from square (6 cm x sin 4.8 degrees = 5 mm) cannot get it either. All of it: 1.0. Success (and the trial's end) needs that full score held with all three boxes still (moving under 1 cm/s and turning under 0.5 rad/s) for 2.5 s. The score is 0 if any box is tilted more than 10 degrees or is off the table (its bottom more than 1 cm below the table top); if the red or green box no longer stands in the channel; if the green box is left of the red one; or if the blue box is over the channel anywhere but standing between the red and green boxes (at the end of the row, or on top of another box).
reset_notes: Stand the red box against the left end stop and the back stop, the green box right next to it against the back stop, and the blue box on the centre of the orange mat, all with their 6 cm side running left to right; tape marks on the strip and the mat make this quick.
fidelity: Approximate: the boxes are solid rigid blocks; real shoe and apparel boxes are hollow, with lids that can catch on a neighbour. Sizes are marked by colour, not printed labels. The channel and mat are fixed in place (screw or tape them down for real trials). Every surface has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), grippier than cardboard on painted steel, so a pushed box slides less readily than a real one.
